questions.question: The total number of particles in a body centred cubic (bcc) unit cell is
questions.answer:
**(B)** two

In a b.c.c. cell there are eight corner atoms, each shared by eight cells, plus one atom wholly inside the body centre:

$$8\times\tfrac18+1=1+1=2$$

So a b.c.c. cell contains **two** atoms. (f.c.c. has $8\times\frac18+6\times\frac12=4$; a simple cube has $8\times\frac18=1$.)

questions.question: Unit of rate constant of third order reaction, $k$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** mol$^{-2}$ L$^2$ s$^{-1}$

For an $n^{th}$-order reaction, $\text{rate}=k[A]^n$, so $k$ has units mol$^{1-n}$ L$^{n-1}$ s$^{-1}$:

$$k=\frac{\text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol L}^{-1})^3}=\text{mol}^{-2}\text{L}^{2}\text{s}^{-1}$$

(First order gives s$^{-1}$, second order mol$^{-1}$ L s$^{-1}$, zero order mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.)

questions.question: CH$_3$-CH$_2$-Cl + NaI $\xrightarrow{\text{acetone},\,\Delta}$ CH$_3$-CH$_2$-I + NaCl. The reaction is
questions.answer:
**(C)** Finkelstein reaction

This is the **Finkelstein reaction**: an alkyl chloride or bromide is refluxed with sodium iodide in dry acetone, and the alkyl iodide is formed because NaI is soluble in acetone while NaCl and NaBr are not — so the precipitation of the sodium halide drives the equilibrium to the right.

$$\ce{CH3CH2Cl + NaI ->[\text{acetone}] CH3CH2I + NaCl v}$$

It is a nucleophilic substitution by I$^-$ (S$_N$2) and is one of the standard ways of preparing alkyl iodides. *(The printed key says Fittig; that is wrong — the Fittig reaction is the coupling of aryl halides with sodium.)*

questions.question: Cuprite is an ore of
questions.answer:
**(B)** Cu

**Cuprite** is copper(I) oxide, **Cu$_2$O** — a red ore of copper, formed in the oxidised upper zones of copper deposits. It is concentrated and then reduced, e.g. by heating with carbon, or leached with dilute sulphuric acid and the copper won by electrolysis:

$$\ce{Cu2O + C -> 2Cu + CO}$$

(Other copper ores: copper pyrite CuFeS$_2$, copper glance Cu$_2$S, malachite CuCO$_3\cdot$Cu(OH)$_2$.)

questions.question: Ethanol + Ethyl chloride → A; 'A' is
questions.answer:
**(B)** Ethyl ethanoate

The question as printed is really the formation of an ester from **ethanol and acetyl chloride**. An acid chloride reacts rapidly with an alcohol (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to give the ester:

$$\ce{CH3COCl + C2H5OH -> CH3COOC2H5 + HCl}$$

Ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate) is the product. *(Read literally — ethanol + ethyl chloride — no reaction occurs without a base; the printed reaction is a misprint for acetyl chloride, and the keyed ester CH$_3$COOC$_2$H$_5$ confirms it.)*

questions.question: Acid chloride is reduced to aldehyde by which of the following?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Rosenmund reduction

Acid chlorides are hydrogenated over a **palladium-on-barium-sulphate catalyst poisoned with sulphur (or quinoline)** to stop the reduction at the aldehyde stage:

$$\ce{RCOCl + H2 ->[Pd/BaSO4][\text{boiled, poison}] RCHO + HCl}$$

The poisoning prevents further reduction of the aldehyde to an alcohol. Wurtz and Fittig reactions are couplings of halides (alkyl and aryl respectively) and form C–C bonds.

questions.question: Enzymes are
questions.answer:
**(B)** Proteins

Except for a few catalytic RNA molecules, **enzymes are proteins** — globular proteins, often conjugated with a non-protein cofactor or coenzyme. Their catalytic power comes from the precise three-dimensional arrangement of amino-acid side chains at the active site, which binds the substrate and lowers the activation energy of a specific reaction. Their activity is lost on denaturation, which is the clearest proof that the protein structure is essential.

questions.question: CH$_3$-CN $\xrightarrow{Na/C_2H_5OH}$ Product, the product is
questions.answer:
**(A)** CH$_3$CH$_2$NH$_2$

Reduction of a nitrile with sodium and ethanol (or LiAlH$_4$, or H$_2$/Ni) adds four hydrogen atoms to the triple bond and gives a **primary amine** with the same number of carbons:

$$\ce{CH3C#N + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NH2}$$

The product is **ethylamine**, a primary amine — the standard method of stepping up the carbon chain by one carbon and ending with an amine.

questions.question: For the reaction 2HI → H$_2$ + I$_2$, what is the order of reaction?
questions.answer:
**Second order** — the rate law for this gas-phase decomposition is

$$\text{rate}=k[\ce{HI}]^2$$

Bimolecular collision between two HI molecules is the rate-determining step, so the reaction is second order overall (and first order in each factor is not the case here). *The balanced equation happens to agree with the experimental order, which is not generally true — order is always determined by experiment.*

questions.question: Write the diseases caused by deficiency of vitamin K.
questions.answer: Deficiency of vitamin K causes **delayed clotting of blood** — prolonged prothrombin time, bleeding gums, easy bruising, and in infants **haemorrhagic disease of the newborn**. Vitamin K is needed by the liver to synthesise prothrombin and several other clotting factors, so its lack shows up as a bleeding tendency rather than a structural disease.

questions.question: What is the particle size of colloidal solution?
questions.answer: The particles in a colloidal solution have diameters from **1 nanometre (10$^{-9}$ m) to 1 micrometre (10$^{-6}$ m)** — i.e. 1–1000 nm. This size is larger than a true solution's molecules but small enough to remain suspended by Brownian motion rather than settle out. Above 1 $\mu$m the particles are coarse enough to settle (a suspension); below 1 nm they form a true solution.

questions.question: What is the use of polyvinyl chloride?
questions.answer:
**PVC (polyvinyl chloride)** is a hard, rigid, chemically resistant plastic used for **pipes, fittings, electrical cable insulation and sheathing, flooring, window frames, bottles and roof sheets**. With plasticisers it becomes the flexible form used for wires, upholstery and rainwear. It is made by addition polymerisation of vinyl chloride:

$$\ce{nCH2=CHCl -> [-CH2-CHCl-]_n}$$

PVC resists acids, alkalis and water, but decomposes slowly on prolonged heating, releasing HCl.

questions.question: Write IUPAC name of CH$_3$C(C$_2$H$_5$)$_2$CH$_2$Br.
questions.answer:
**1-bromo-2-ethyl-2-methylbutane**

Expanding the condensed formula: $\ce{BrCH2-C(CH3)(C2H5)2}$, i.e. carbon 2 carries a methyl and two ethyl groups and the Br is on C-1. The longest chain must include the carbon bearing Br and the longest available chain through C-2 — that is a **butane** chain (C-2, one ethyl and C-1):

$$\ce{BrCH2-C(CH3)(C2H5)-CH2CH3}$$

Numbering from the Br end gives bromo at C-1, and the substituents at C-2 are one methyl and one ethyl. Alphabetically ethyl comes first: **1-bromo-2-ethyl-2-methylbutane**. (The printed key writes '1-bromo-2-ethyle-2-methylbutane', a spelling slip.)

questions.question: Give one example of oligosaccharides.
questions.answer:
**Sucrose** (cane sugar) — a disaccharide made of one glucose and one fructose unit joined by a glycosidic linkage; other examples are **lactose** (glucose + galactose) and **maltose** (two glucose units).

Oligosaccharides are carbohydrates that yield 2–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis, so sucrose, with two units, is the simplest common example. (Raffinose, with three units, is another.)

questions.question: Give an example of antibiotic.
questions.answer:
**Penicillin** (benzylpenicillin) — a $\beta$-lactam antibiotic obtained from *Penicillium notatum*, which kills bacteria by inhibiting the transpeptidase enzyme that cross-links their cell walls. Other examples: **streptomycin**, **chloramphenicol**, **tetracycline**, **erythromycin**.

Antibiotics are substances produced by micro-organisms (or made synthetically) that inhibit the growth of, or destroy, other micro-organisms; they are not effective against viruses. (The printed key's answer, 'penicillin-resistance enterococcus', names a resistant organism rather than an antibiotic.)

questions.question: Distinguish between electronic conduction and electrolytic conduction.
questions.answer:
| Electronic (metallic) conduction | Electrolytic conduction |
|---|---|
| Due to the movement of **electrons** | Due to the movement of **ions** |
| No chemical change in the conductor | Involves decomposition of the electrolyte — a chemical change at the electrodes |
| No transfer of matter | Transfer of matter (ions) through the solution |
| Conductance **decreases** with rising temperature (lattice vibrations scatter electrons) | Conductance **increases** with rising temperature (more ions, greater mobility) |
| Conductivity is generally high (10$^4$–10$^5$ S cm$^{-1}$) | Conductivity is low and rises with dilution |
| Examples: copper, graphite | Examples: NaCl solution, molten NaCl |

questions.question: Explain the following: (a) Metallurgy (b) Flux
questions.answer:
**(a) Metallurgy** is the branch of science and technology concerned with the extraction of metals from their ores and their purification. It covers the whole sequence: crushing and concentration of the ore, conversion to the oxide (roasting or calcination), reduction to the crude metal, and refining (electrolytic, zone or vapour-phase).

**(b) A flux** is a substance added during smelting to combine with the infusible impurities (gangue) of an ore and form a **fusible slag** that can be run off. If the impurity is acidic (silica) a **basic flux** such as CaO is used; if the impurity is basic a acidic flux such as SiO$_2$ is used:

$$\ce{CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3}$$

The slag is lighter than the molten metal and floats on it, so the two are easily separated.

questions.question: Why does NH$_3$ form hydrogen bonding while PH$_3$ does not?
questions.answer:
Hydrogen bonding needs **a small, highly electronegative atom (N, O, F) bearing a hydrogen** so that the H carries a large partial positive charge and can be attracted to a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.

In **ammonia** nitrogen is small and strongly electronegative (3.0), so the N–H bond is strongly polarised, the H is appreciably $\delta+$, and each N–H can hydrogen-bond to the lone pair of another NH$_3$. Hence NH$_3$ has a high boiling point (−33 °C) and is very soluble in water.

In **phosphine** phosphorus is larger and much less electronegative (2.1); the P–H bond is almost non-polar, so the hydrogen carries little positive charge and the molecule is essentially non-polar. With weak dipole–dipole forces and no hydrogen bonds, PH$_3$ is a gas (b.p. −88 °C) and almost insoluble in water. *(The printed answer garbles 'N' as 'V'.)*

questions.question: Predict which of the following ions will be coloured in aqueous solution. Give reason for each: Cu$^+$ and Fe$^{3+}$
questions.answer:
**Cu$^+$: colourless (and unstable in water).** Cu$^+$ is $3d^{10}$ — a completely filled d subshell — so there is no unpaired electron and no possible $d$–$d$ transition in the visible region. In aqueous solution, however, Cu(I) disproportionates:

$$\ce{2Cu^+ -> Cu^2+ + Cu}$$

which is why 'Cu$^+$ solutions' are rarely seen.

**Fe$^{3+}$: coloured (pale yellow to violet depending on the ligands).** Fe$^{3+}$ is $3d^5$ — an incompletely filled d subshell with five unpaired electrons. Absorption of visible light promotes an electron between the split d orbitals ($d$–$d$ transition), so the ion is coloured; the aqueous ion $[\ce{Fe(H2O)6}]^{3+}$ is pale violet, becoming yellow-brown as hydrolysis gives hydroxy complexes.

*Note on the printed key:* the book writes 'Cu$^+$ ion has $3d^{10}$ configuration' — correct — but then cites Fe$^{3+}$ as having a 'pale violet' colour for the right reason; the printed option (a) answer is thus misleading if read as Cu$^{2+}$ (which **is** blue, being $3d^9$).

questions.question: Complete the following: (a) $\ce{CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc) ->}$ (b) $\ce{C2H5Cl + C2H5ONa ->}$
questions.answer:
**(a) Dehydrohalogenation** (alcoholic KOH):

$$\ce{CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc) -> CH2=CH2 ^ + KBr + H2O}$$

**Ethene** is evolved. Because the medium is a base rather than a nucleophile, elimination (E2) competes with and wins over substitution.

**(b) Williamson ether synthesis:**

$$\ce{C2H5Cl + C2H5ONa -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + NaCl}$$

**Diethyl ether** is formed — the alkoxide ion attacks the carbon carrying the halogen in an S$_N$2 displacement, which is the general laboratory method for making symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers.

questions.question: What happens when glucose is treated with the following reagents? (a) HI (b) Bromine water
questions.answer:
**(a) With HI:** glucose is reduced by prolonged heating with concentrated hydriodic acid, all the oxygen being removed as water and the carbon skeleton hydrogenated. n-Hexane (with some 2-iodohexane) is obtained:

$$\ce{C6H12O6 + 6HI ->[\Delta] C6H14 + 3I2 + 3H2O}$$

This proves that glucose is a straight-chain six-carbon compound with the carbons linked in an unbranched sequence.

**(b) With bromine water:** bromine water is a mild oxidising agent; it oxidises the aldehyde group of glucose to a carboxyl group without touching the secondary hydroxyls, giving **gluconic acid**:

$$\ce{CH2OH(CHOH)4CHO + Br2 + H2O -> CH2OH(CHOH)4COOH + 2HBr}$$

(The cyclic hemiacetal ring opens for this reaction; the result confirms that glucose is an aldose, since ketoses are not oxidised by bromine water.)

questions.question: Write any two differences between thermoplastics and thermosetting polymers.
questions.answer:
| Thermoplastics | Thermosetting polymers |
|---|---|
| Soften on heating and can be remoulded repeatedly | Set on heating and cannot be remoulded — they char instead |
| Linear or branched long chains held by weak van der Waals forces | Cross-linked three-dimensional networks held by strong covalent bonds |
| Formed by **addition** polymerisation | Usually formed by **condensation** polymerisation |
| Generally soft and flexible | Hard, rigid and brittle |
| Examples: polythene, PVC, polystyrene | Examples: bakelite, melamine, urea–formaldehyde resin |

questions.question: Write briefly with one example: (a) Disinfectants (b) Antacids
questions.answer:
**(a) Disinfectants** are chemicals that kill micro-organisms but are too strong or corrosive to be applied to living tissue, so they are used only on **non-living objects** — floors, drains, instruments, excreta. Example: **phenol (1% solution)**; also bleaching powder, Dettol, and hypochlorite solutions.

**(b) Antacids** are substances that **neutralise the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach** and so relieve hyperacidity and the pain of peptic ulcer, raising the gastric pH to a comfortable level. Example: **sodium hydrogen carbonate, $\ce{NaHCO3}$**; also aluminium hydroxide gel and magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), which are preferred because they do not generate CO$_2$.

questions.question: Write the properties of transition elements with reference to (a) oxidation state (b) magnetic properties.
questions.answer:
**(a) Oxidation states.** Transition metals show **variable oxidation states**, because the energies of the $ns$ and $(n-1)d$ orbitals are so close that electrons from both can take part in bonding. The lowest states arise when only $ns$ electrons are used (e.g. +2 for Fe, Mn); higher states involve $d$ electrons as well, up to the loss of all of them (+7 for Mn in permanganate). The stability of a particular state varies across the series — Mn(II) and Fe(III) are stable, while Co(III) is strongly oxidising and Cr(VI) is a powerful oxidising state in acid.

**(b) Magnetic properties.** These follow from unpaired d electrons:

- **Paramagnetism** — when the ion has one or more unpaired d electrons (e.g. $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, $d^9$, one unpaired electron; $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$, $d^5$, five). The magnetic moment is given by $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ B.M.
- **Diamagnetism** — when all electrons are paired (e.g. $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$, $d^{10}$; $\ce{Ti^{4+}}$, $d^0$).

In octahedral complexes, weak-field ligands give **high-spin** and strong-field ligands **low-spin** arrangements, so the same ion can be paramagnetic or diamagnetic depending on its ligands — e.g. $[\ce{Fe(CN)6}]^{3-}$ has one unpaired electron while $[\ce{Fe(H2O)6}]^{3+}$ has five.

questions.question: Differentiate between order and molecularity of reaction.
questions.answer:
| Order of reaction | Molecularity of reaction |
|---|---|
| The sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimentally determined **rate equation** | The number of reacting species that collide simultaneously in an **elementary step** |
| Determined **experimentally** | Derived from the **mechanism**; a theoretical concept |
| Obtained from the rate law | Obtained from the reaction step |
| May be zero, integral or **fractional** | Always a **whole number** (1, 2, 3) |
| Applies to complex as well as elementary reactions | Applies only to elementary reactions |
| Can be zero (e.g. photochemical $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$) | Cannot be zero |

Order is a measured quantity and can change with conditions; molecularity is a property of a single step, so a complex reaction has **no** molecularity, only an order.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (a) Adsorbent (b) Brownian movement
questions.answer:
**(a) Adsorbent.** The **solid on whose surface adsorption occurs** — the substance that takes up the other species. E.g. in the adsorption of a gas by charcoal, charcoal is the adsorbent and the gas is the adsorbate. Good adsorbents are highly porous solids with a large surface area per gram, such as activated charcoal, silica gel and alumina.

**(b) Brownian movement.** The **continuous, random, zig-zag motion of the dispersed-phase particles of a colloidal sol**, first observed by Robert Brown in 1828 with pollen grains in water. It arises from the unequal, random bombardment of the particles by the molecules of the dispersion medium. Brownian motion keeps the particles suspended against gravity and is direct evidence for the kinetic theory of matter.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following transformations? (a) Ethyl alcohol to Ethyl chloride (b) Acetylene to acetaldehyde (c) Aniline to Benzene diazonium chloride
questions.answer:
**(a) Ethyl alcohol → ethyl chloride:**

$$\ce{C2H5OH + HCl ->[\text{anhyd. }ZnCl2] C2H5Cl + H2O}$$

(Lucas reagent; also $\ce{PCl5}$ or $\ce{SOCl2}$ give the same product.)

**(b) Acetylene → acetaldehyde:** hydration of ethyne gives vinyl alcohol, which tautomerises to acetaldehyde:

$$\ce{C2H2 + H2O ->[H2SO4][HgSO4] CH2=CHOH <=> CH3CHO}$$

The enol form is unstable and rearranges; the overall Markovnikov addition puts the OH on the more substituted carbon.

**(c) Aniline → benzene diazonium chloride:** diazotisation in the cold:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl ->[273-278 K] C6H5N2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H2O}$$

Nitrous acid is generated *in situ*; the temperature must be kept below 278 K or the salt decomposes to phenol.

questions.question: Using IUPAC norms, write the formulae for the following: (a) hexa-ammine cobalt (III) sulphate (b) tetra-aquodichlorido-chromium (III) ion (c) potassium dicyanoargentate (I)
questions.answer:
**(a) Hexaamminecobalt(III) sulphate:** the cation is $[\ce{Co(NH3)6}]^{3+}$ and sulphate is $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$, so two cations balance three sulphates:

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]2(SO4)3}$$

**(b) Tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) ion:** four H$_2$O, two Cl$^-$ and Cr$^{3+}$:

$$\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]^+}$$

Charge: $+3+0+2(-1)=+1$.

**(c) Potassium dicyanoargentate(I):** $[\ce{Ag(CN)2}]^-$ with one K$^+$:

$$\ce{K[Ag(CN)2]}$$

Charge: $+1+2(-1)=-1$, balanced by K$^+$. (The printed key's KAg(CN)$_2$ is the same formula.)

questions.question: What is salt bridge? Mention its functions.
questions.answer:
A **salt bridge** is an inverted U-tube (or a strip of filter paper) filled with a concentrated solution of an inert electrolyte such as **KCl or $\ce{KNO3}$**, often set in agar-agar gel, which connects the two half-cells of a galvanic cell.

**Functions:**

1. It **completes the internal circuit**, allowing charge to flow between the half-cells so that the cell can deliver current continuously.
2. It **prevents the transference of electrolytes** (the two solutions) from one half-cell to the other, so the two electrode solutions do not mix.
3. It **maintains electrical neutrality**: as Zn$^{2+}$ is produced at the anode and Cu$^{2+}$ is consumed at the cathode, Cl$^-$ migrates towards the anode compartment and K$^+$ towards the cathode compartment, keeping each solution neutral.

KCl is chosen because K$^+$ and Cl$^-$ have almost equal mobilities, so no liquid-junction potential is set up.

questions.question: Predict the product: (a) $\ce{CHCl3 + O2 ->[light]}$ (b) $\ce{CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 ->[85\% H3PO4][440 K]}$ (c) phthalic acid with CHO and COOH $\xrightarrow{NaCN/HCl}$
questions.answer:
**(a)** Chloroform is oxidised by air in the presence of light to the poisonous gas **phosgene**:

$$\ce{2CHCl3 + O2 ->[h\nu] 2COCl2 + 2HCl}$$

(which is why chloroform is stored in dark bottles with a little ethanol to destroy any phosgene).

**(b)** Propan-2-ol is **dehydrated** to propene:

$$\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3 ->[85\%\ H3PO4][440 K] CH3CH=CH2 + H2O}$$

**(c)** o-Formylbenzoic acid (2-formylbenzoic acid) condensed with NaCN/HCl gives the **cyanohydrin**, which cyclises to a lactone — the product is the cyanohydrin **2-(1-hydroxy-1-cyanomethyl)benzoic acid**, the intermediate in the synthesis of 3-substituted phthalides. In the printed answer the structure drawn adds HCN across the aldehyde to give $\ce{-CH(OH)CN}$ while the —COOH remains free.

questions.question: Complete the following reactions: (a) $\ce{XeF4 + H2 ->}$ (b) $\ce{XeF4 + Pt ->}$ (c) $\ce{XeOF4 + 3H2 ->}$
questions.answer:
**(a)**

$$\ce{XeF4 + 2H2 -> Xe + 4HF}$$

**(b)**

$$\ce{XeF4 + Pt -> PtF4 + Xe}$$

Xenon tetrafluoride is a strong fluorinating agent — it will even fluorinate platinum metal, being reduced to xenon.

**(c)**

$$\ce{XeOF4 + 3H2 -> Xe + H2O + 4HF}$$

All three reactions reduce xenon to the free element. Note that xenon fluorides are powerful oxidising and fluorinating agents precisely because xenon is in a high, unstable positive oxidation state (+4 and +6) and readily returns to Xe(0).

questions.question: An antifreeze solution is prepared from 222.6 g of ethylene glycol, C$_2$H$_4$(OH)$_2$, and 200 g of water. Calculate the molality of the solution. If the density of the solution is 1.072 g mL$^{-1}$, then what shall be the molarity of the solution?
questions.answer:
**Molar mass of ethylene glycol** $\ce{C2H6O2} = 2(12)+6(1)+2(16)=62\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

$$n=\frac{222.6}{62}=3.59\ \text{mol}$$

**Molality** (moles of solute per kg of *solvent*):

$$m=\frac{3.59}{0.200}=17.95\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}\approx18\ \text{m}$$

**Molarity.** Mass of solution $=222.6+200=422.6$ g, so

$$V=\frac{m}{\rho}=\frac{422.6}{1.072}=394.2\ \text{mL}=0.3942\ \text{L}$$

$$M=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{3.59}{0.3942}=9.11\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**Molality ≈ 17.95 m, molarity ≈ 9.11 M.** The two differ so much because ethylene glycol is a large fraction of the mixture and the solution is denser than water; molality counts only the water (200 g) while molarity uses the whole solution volume.

questions.question: How is phosphine prepared in laboratory? How does it react with (a) CuSO$_4$ and (b) HgCl$_2$? / Discuss the general characteristics of group 16 elements with reference to (a) atomic size, (b) ionisation enthalpy and (c) electronegativity.
questions.answer:
**Preparation of phosphine.** White phosphorus is heated with a strong solution of caustic soda in an atmosphere of carbon dioxide (air must be excluded, since PH$_3$ is spontaneously flammable):

$$\ce{P4 + 3NaOH + 3H2O -> 3NaH2PO2 + PH3 ^}$$

Sodium hypophosphite is the other product. The gas is passed through a freezing mixture to condense P$_2$H$_4$ (which makes it spontaneously inflammable) and dried.

**(a) With CuSO$_4$** — phosphine gives a black precipitate of **copper phosphide**:

$$\ce{2PH3 + 3CuSO4 -> Cu3P2 v + 3H2SO4}$$

**(b) With HgCl$_2$** — mercuric phosphide is formed:

$$\ce{2PH3 + 3HgCl2 -> Hg3P2 v + 6HCl}$$

This is the basis of the test that distinguishes PH$_3$ from other gases.

**Group 16 characteristics.**

**(a) Atomic size.** Atomic radii increase down the group (O < S < Se < Te < Po) as new shells are added; they are smaller than those of the corresponding group-15 elements at the same period, because the greater nuclear charge at constant shielding contracts the atom.

**(b) Ionisation enthalpy.** It decreases down the group for the same reason, but the values for group 16 are **higher** than for the corresponding group-15 elements — the extra electron has entered the same shell without new shielding, so the effective nuclear charge is larger and the electrons are held more tightly.

**(c) Electronegativity.** It decreases down the group. **Oxygen is the second most electronegative element after fluorine** (3.44), because of its very small size; the value falls steadily to tellurium, which is why the elements become more metallic and the hydrides less acidic down the group.

questions.question: Write short notes on the following: (a) Carbylamine reaction (b) Hoffmann's bromamide reaction (c) Gattermann reaction. / Identify 'X', 'Y' and 'Z': (a) $\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[conc. H2SO4][443 K] X ->[H2O+O][alk. KMnO4]}$ (b) $\ce{CH3CHBrCH3 ->[KOH(alc)] X' ->[HBr][\text{peroxide}] Y' ->[Cl2][h\nu] Z'}$
questions.answer:
**(a) Carbylamine reaction.** Primary amines — aliphatic or aromatic — on warming with chloroform and alcoholic KOH give the foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine):

$$\ce{C2H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH ->[\Delta] C2H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

It is the standard test for a primary amine; secondary and tertiary amines do not respond.

**(b) Hoffmann's bromamide reaction.** An amide is treated with bromine and alkali, and loses its carbonyl group to give a primary amine with **one carbon less**:

$$\ce{RCONH2 + Br2 + 4KOH -> RNH2 + K2CO3 + 2KBr + 2H2O}$$

So ethanamide gives methanamine. The mechanism goes through an N-bromoamide and an isocyanate, and the alkyl group migrates to nitrogen.

**(c) Gattermann reaction.** A benzene diazonium salt is treated with copper powder and the corresponding halogen acid, giving the aryl halide — the same transformation as the Sandmeyer reaction but with copper metal instead of a copper(I) halide:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + HCl ->[Cu] C6H5Cl + N2 + HCl}$$

**Identifying X, Y, Z.**

(a) Ethanol is dehydrated to **ethene**, which is oxidised by alkaline KMnO$_4$ to **ethylene glycol**:

$$\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[conc. H2SO4][443 K] CH2=CH2 (X) ->[H2O+O][KMnO4] HOCH2CH2OH}$$

So **X = ethene, $\ce{CH2=CH2}$**; the final product is ethylene glycol (ethane-1,2-diol).

(b) 2-Bromopropane is dehydrohalogenated to **propene (X′)**, and anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr with peroxide gives **1-bromopropane (Y′)**, which on photochemical chlorination gives **1-chloropropane / 1,1-dichloropropane (Z′)** by free-radical substitution:

$$\ce{CH3CHBrCH3 ->[KOH(alc)] CH3CH=CH2 ->[HBr/\text{peroxide}] CH3CH2CH2Br ->[Cl2][h\nu] CH3CH2CH2Cl + HCl}$$

So **X′ = propene, Y′ = 1-bromopropane, Z′ = 1-chloropropane**.
